elements.quote: This is the first edition of a living systematic review of randomized clinical trials comparing the effects of all treatment interventions for participants in all age groups with COVID-19.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly identifies the report as a (living) systematic review.

elements.quote: a living systematic review of randomized clinical trials comparing the effects of all treatment interventions for participants in all age groups with COVID-19
elements.reason: The review objective (comparing effects of all treatment interventions for COVID-19) is clearly stated in the abstract.

elements.quote: randomized clinical trials comparing the effects of all treatment interventions for participants in all age groups with COVID-19
elements.reason: The abstract implies inclusion of RCTs in COVID-19 participants of all age groups, but explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria are not detailed.

elements.quote: We searched relevant databases and websites for published and unpublished trials until August 7, 2020.
elements.reason: The abstract reports when sources were last searched (August 7, 2020) but does not name the specific information sources.

elements.quote: Two reviewers independently extracted data and assessed trial methodology.
elements.reason: The abstract mentions that trial methodology was assessed by two reviewers independently, but does not specify the risk of bias tool or method used.

elements.quote: We planned to conduct aggregate data meta-analyses, trial sequential analyses, network meta-analysis, and individual patient data meta-analyses... We performed both fixed-effect and random-effects meta-analyses.
elements.reason: The abstract specifies the synthesis methods (meta-analyses, trial sequential analyses) used to present and synthesize results.

elements.quote: We included 33 randomized clinical trials enrolling a total of 13,312 participants. All trials were at overall high risk of bias.
elements.reason: The abstract reports the total number of included studies (33), participants (13,312), and relevant characteristics (high risk of bias).

elements.quote: This trial showed evidence of a beneficial effect of dexamethasone on all-cause mortality (rate ratio 0.83; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.750.93; p < 0.001; low certainty) and on mechanical ventilation (risk ratio [RR] 0.77; 95% CI 0.62-0.95; p = 0.021; low certainty).
elements.reason: The abstract presents results for the main outcomes (all-cause mortality, serious adverse events, mechanical ventilation, etc.) with effect estimates.

elements.quote: Meta-analysis showed no evidence of a difference between remdesivir versus placebo on all-cause mortality (RR 0.74; 95% CI 0.40-1.37; p = 0.34, I 2 = 58%; 2 trials; very low certainty)
elements.reason: The abstract reports summary estimates with confidence intervals for the conducted meta-analyses.

elements.quote: Meta-analysis showed evidence of a beneficial effect of remdesivir versus placebo on serious adverse events (RR 0.77; 95% CI 0.63-0.94; p = 0.009, I 2 = 0%; 2 trials; very low certainty)
elements.reason: The abstract indicates direction of effect and which group is favored (e.g., 'beneficial effect of remdesivir', 'harmful effect on nonserious adverse events' for hydroxychloroquine).

elements.quote: The main limitation of this living review is the paucity of data currently available. Furthermore, the included trials were all at risks of systematic errors and random errors.
elements.reason: The abstract briefly summarizes important limitations (paucity of data, risk of bias/random errors).

elements.quote: Five single trials showed statistically significant results but were underpowered to confirm or reject realistic intervention effects.
elements.reason: The abstract provides limited interpretation (e.g., underpowered trials, low certainty), but a general interpretation of results and their implications is only partially developed.

elements.quote: SJ, JCJ, and CG received a grant from The Grundfos Foundation (Grant number: 2020025
elements.reason: The funding statement appears within the abstract section (PLOS 'Methods And Findings' abstract block), identifying the funding sources.

elements.quote: our protocol [9], which was registered in the PROSPERO database (ID: CRD42020178787)
elements.reason: Registration (PROSPERO CRD42020178787) is reported in the Methods section, not in the abstract; the abstract itself does not provide the register name and registration number.

elements.quote: No evidence-based treatment for COVID-19 currently exist to augment widely used supportive care protocols [7]. ... Many randomized clinical trials assessing the effects of different potential treatments for COVID-19 are currently underway.
elements.reason: The Introduction describes the current state of knowledge (no evidence-based treatment, many trials underway) and the uncertainty this creates.

elements.quote: there is an urgent need to continuously surveil and update the aggregated evidence base so that effective interventions, if such exist, are implemented in clinical practice [8]. The present living systematic review with aggregate meta-analyses and trial sequential analyses aims to continuously inform evidence-based guideline recommendations for the treatment of COVID-19
elements.reason: The importance and need for the review are explicitly explained in the Introduction.

elements.quote: Wehave identified 4 important reviews that are comparable to our present project [77-80].
elements.reason: Similar existing reviews are identified and cited, and the need for the current review relative to them is explained, but this appears in the Discussion rather than the Introduction/rationale section.
No proposed mechanism of action for the assessed interventions (e.g., antivirals, corticosteroids) is described in the retrieved evidence.
The review evaluates individual pharmacological interventions for COVID-19, not complex interventions or delivery contexts, so a logic model is not required.

elements.quote: There is a need for a living systematic review evaluating the beneficial and harmful effects of all possible interventions for treatment of COVID-19.
elements.reason: The rationale section states the review aims to evaluate beneficial and harmful effects of interventions for COVID-19, which conveys the objective, but no explicit, formal statement of objectives or questions (e.g., 'The objective of this review was...') is present in the retrieved evidence.

This is a review of intervention effects, so planned comparisons apply, but the retrieved evidence contains no PICO (or variant) formulation of populations, interventions, comparators, or planned comparisons; only outcomes are listed (text_13), and the objectives are said to be detailed in the protocol, which is not provided.

elements.quote: a living systematic review of randomized clinical trials comparing the effects of all treatment interventions for participants in all age groups with COVID-19
elements.reason: Study design (RCTs), population (all age groups with COVID-19), and interventions (all treatments) are stated, but no full explicit eligibility criteria (settings, follow-up requirements, diagnostic criteria) are detailed in the retrieved evidence; details deferred to the protocol.

elements.quote: Trials were included irrespective of language, publication status, publication year, and publication type.
elements.reason: Report characteristics (language, publication status, year, type) are explicitly specified.

No distinction is made between exclusion because outcomes were not measured versus not reported; the only exclusion-related note concerns unusable reporting of results (text_22), which does not address this distinction.

elements.quote: Primary and secondary outcomes were predefined in our protocol [9]... We planned several subgroup analyses, which are described in detail in our protocol [9].
elements.reason: Comparisons used in syntheses appear from results (e.g., intervention versus standard care/placebo), and subgroup analyses are mentioned but deferred to the protocol; the groups for each synthesis are not fully specified and linked in the Methods text.
No notable restrictions on eligibility (e.g., language or publication limits) were imposed, so no rationale for restrictions is required.

elements.quote: We searched all databases from their inception and until August 7, 2020.
elements.reason: The date when the sources were last searched is explicitly reported (August 7, 2020).

elements.quote: searched the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) in The Cochrane Library, Medical Literature Analysis and Retrieval System Online (MEDLINE Ovid), Excerpta Medica database (Embase Ovid), Latin American and Caribbean Health Sciences Literature (LILACS; Bireme), Science Citation Index Expanded (SCI-EXPANDED; Web of Science)... CINAHL (EBSCO host)... We searched all databases from their inception and until August 7, 2020.
elements.reason: Database names, platforms/interfaces (Ovid, Bireme, Web of Science, EBSCO), and coverage dates (inception to August 7, 2020) are all reported.

elements.quote: we searched clinical trial registries (e.g., clinicaltrials.gov, clinicaltrialregister.eu, who.int/ictrp, chictr.org.cn) of Europe, USA, and China, and websites of pharmaceutical companies, websites of US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and European Medicines Agency (EMA). We also searched the COVID-19 Study Registry [13] and the real-time dashboard of randomized trials [14].
elements.reason: Registries and repositories are named, but no date restrictions or last-searched dates specific to these registers are reported; the August 7, 2020 date applies to 'all databases'.

elements.quote: websites of pharmaceutical companies, websites of US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and European Medicines Agency (EMA). We also searched... preprint servers (bioRxiv, medRxiv)

No organisations or manufacturers are reported as contacted to identify studies; pharmaceutical company websites were searched, not the companies contacted.

elements.quote: The reference lists of relevant trial publications were checked for any unidentified randomized clinical trials.

elements.quote: Electronic searches... Searching other resources. The reference lists of relevant trial publications were checked...

elements.reason: Disagreement resolution process is described, including third-author consultation.

elements.reason: Process for obtaining/confirming data from study investigators is described.
No evidence of automation tools used for data collection; manual extraction with a standardized sheet was reported, so this conditional item does not apply.

elements.quote: Primary outcomes were all-cause mortality and serious adverse events (as defined by the International Conference on Harmonation-Good Clinical Practice [ICH-GCP] guidelines) [9,16]. Secondary outcomes were admission to intensive care (as defined by trialists), receipt of mechanical ventilation (as defined by trialists), receipt of renal replacement therapy (as defined by trialists), quality of life, and nonserious adverse events. We classified nonserious adverse events as any adverse event not assessed as serious according to the ICH-GCP definition.
elements.reason: All primary and secondary outcome domains are listed and defined, including definitions referencing ICH-GCP and trialist definitions.

elements.quote: For all outcomes, we used the trial results reported at maximum follow-up.
elements.reason: The time frame of measurement is specified as trial results at maximum follow-up for all outcomes.
The manuscript does not explicitly state whether all compatible results (all measures, time points, analyses) within each outcome domain were sought.
The manuscript does not indicate that only a subset of compatible results was sought, so no selection process needed describing.

elements.quote: Further, we included 'time to clinical improvement' as an outcome post hoc.
elements.reason: The post hoc addition of an outcome is reported, but no rationale for the change is provided.
No changes to processes for selecting results within outcome domains are reported in the retrieved evidence.

Although primary and secondary outcomes are distinguished, no explicit statement identifies which outcomes were considered most important for interpreting conclusions or the rationale for their prioritisation.

elements.quote: Primary outcomes were all-cause mortality and serious adverse events (as defined by the International Conference on Harmonation-Good Clinical Practice [ICH-GCP] guidelines) [9,16]. Secondary outcomes were admission to intensive care (as defined by trialists), receipt of mechanical ventilation (as defined by trialists), receipt of renal replacement therapy (as defined by trialists), quality of life, and nonserious adverse events.
elements.reason: Outcome variables are listed and defined (including ICH-GCP definitions), but other data items such as participant characteristics, intervention characteristics, and funding sources of included studies are not explicitly listed as variables for which data were sought.
The manuscript mentions contacting trial authors when data were unclear or missing (text_11), but no assumptions made about missing or unclear information are described.

No tool or reference used to determine which data items to collect (e.g., a data collection form template or guide) is cited; only a 'standardized data extraction sheet' is mentioned without citation.

elements.quote: Risk of bias was assessed with the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool-version 2 (RoB 2) [12,15].
elements.reason: The tool and version (Cochrane RoB 2) are explicitly specified.

elements.quote: Bias was assessed with the following domains: bias arising from the randomization process, bias due to deviations from the intended interventions, bias due to missing outcome data, bias in measurement of outcomes, and bias arising from selective reporting of results [12,15].
elements.reason: All five RoB 2 domains assessed are listed.

elements.quote: All trials were assessed as at high risk of bias ( S3 Table ).
elements.reason: Overall risk-of-bias judgements are reported (all trials at high risk; see also text_2), but the rules used to derive the overall judgement are not described.

elements.quote: Risk of bias was assessed with the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool-version 2 (RoB 2) [12,15].
elements.reason: The standard RoB 2 tool was used with its stated domains; no adaptations to the tool are reported.

elements.quote: Risk of bias was assessed with the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool-version 2 (RoB 2) [12,15].
elements.reason: Only an existing tool (RoB 2) was used; no new tool was developed.

elements.quote: Six authors in pairs (SJ, EEN, JF, FS, CKJ, EB) independently assessed risk of bias. Any discrepancies were resolved through discussion or, if required, through discussion with a third author (JCJ).
elements.reason: Number of reviewers, independent paired assessment, and disagreement-resolution procedures are reported.

elements.quote: Wecontacted authors of trials with unclear or missing data.
elements.reason: The process of contacting trial authors to obtain or confirm information is described, albeit briefly.

elements.quote: Six authors in pairs (SJ, EEN, JF, FS, CKJ, EB) independently assessed risk of bias.
elements.reason: Risk of bias was assessed manually by authors; no automation tools are reported or implied.

elements.quote: We used risk ratios (RRs) for dichotomous outcomes. We planned to calculate the mean differences (MDs) and standardized mean difference (SMD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) for continuous outcomes.
elements.reason: Methods specify effect measures by outcome type: RRs for dichotomous outcomes and MD/SMD for continuous outcomes.

elements.quote: We assessed a total of 2 primary outcomes, and we therefore adjusted our thresholds for significance [18] and considered a p-value of 0.033 or less as the threshold for statistical significance [9,18].
elements.reason: Thresholds for interpreting significance are reported with rationale (adjustment for two primary outcomes); TSA also uses a 20% relative risk reduction assumption.
No evidence describes re-expressing synthesized results using another effect measure.

elements.quote: We conducted both random-effects (Inverse Variance, DerSimonian-Laird) and fixed-effect (Mantel-Haenszel) meta-analyses for all analyses and chose the most conservative result as our primary result [12,18,21,22].
elements.reason: Choice of analysis model is justified by reference to conservative-result selection and cited methods, but no explicit justification for choosing RR/MD as effect measures is provided.

The retrieved evidence describes data extraction, outcomes, and statistical synthesis methods, but no process is described for deciding which studies were eligible for each synthesis (e.g., tabulating study intervention characteristics and comparing them against planned synthesis groups). The comparisons are only listed retrospectively in the Results section (text_15), not as an eligibility-decision process in the Methods.

elements.quote: We used risk ratios (RRs) for dichotomous outcomes. We planned to calculate the mean differences (MDs) and standardized mean difference (SMD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) for continuous outcomes.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes some data preparation/conversion choices (effect measure selection for dichotomous and continuous outcomes) and mentions contacting trial authors when data were unclear or missing (text_11, text_12), but it does not explicitly describe handling of missing summary statistics or detailed data conversion procedures (e.g., imputation or unit conversions).

The retrieved evidence lists many tables (e.g., 'S4 Table. Summary of findings table of dexamethasone versus standard care') but the Methods section contains no description of the tabular structures used to display results or the data included in them.

elements.quote: Trial sequential analysis showed that we did not have enough information to confirm or reject that remdesivir versus placebo reduces all-cause mortality with a relative risk reduction of 20% [9] ( Fig 3 ).
elements.reason: Graphical displays (forest plots and trial sequential analysis figures) are used and their content is explained in detail in figure captions (e.g., Fig 3 caption describing the Z-curve, boundaries, and DARIS), but the Methods section never explicitly describes the graphical methods used to display results.
No evidence reports the basis for ordering or grouping studies within tables or graphs (e.g., the forest plot in figure_4 lists studies by name with no stated ordering rationale).
Trial sequential analysis figures are non-standard graphs, but no rationale for using this graphical display format is reported in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: Review Manager version 5.4 (The Nordic Cochrane Centre, The Cochrane Collaboration, Copenhagen, Denmark) [19] and Stata 16 (StataCorp LLC, College Station, TX, USA) [20] were used for all statistical analyses.
elements.reason: Software packages and version numbers (Review Manager 5.4, Stata 16) explicitly reported.

elements.quote: Because of the lack of relevant data, it was not possible to perform other meta-analyses, network meta-analysis, or individual patient data meta-analyses.
elements.reason: Alternative approach (single trial results, narrative summary) described; reasons for inability to perform planned syntheses given.

elements.quote: We conducted both randomeffects (Inverse Variance, DerSimonian-Laird) and fixed-effect (Mantel-Haenszel) meta-analyses for all analyses and chose the most conservative result as our primary result [12,18,21,22].
elements.reason: Models (random-effects and fixed-effect) reported with rationale (choosing most conservative result).

elements.quote: We used risk ratios (RRs) for dichotomous outcomes. We planned to calculate the mean differences (MDs) and standardized mean difference (SMD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) for continuous outcomes.
elements.reason: Statistical methods (Inverse Variance, DerSimonian-Laird, Mantel-Haenszel, effect measures) reported.

elements.quote: Statistical heterogeneity was quantified by calculating inconsistency (I square) for traditional meta-analyses and diversity (D square) for trial sequential analysis.
elements.reason: Heterogeneity assessment methods (I2 and D2) explicitly described.

elements.quote: randomeffects (Inverse Variance, DerSimonian-Laird)
elements.reason: Between-study variance estimator (DerSimonian-Laird) reported for random-effects meta-analysis.

elements.quote: We planned to calculate the mean differences (MDs) and standardized mean difference (SMD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) for continuous outcomes.
elements.reason: 95% CIs reported for effect estimates, but the specific method for calculating CI around the random-effects summary effect is not explicitly stated.

elements.quote: We conducted both randomeffects (Inverse Variance, DerSimonian-Laird) and fixed-effect (Mantel-Haenszel) meta-analyses for all analyses and chose the most conservative result as our primary result
elements.reason: Implementation details partially covered (both models run, conservative result chosen), but no further random-effects implementation details (e.g., continuity corrections) reported.
No Bayesian meta-analysis was performed; frequentist methods and trial sequential analysis were used.
No methods for handling statistical dependency among multiple estimates from the same study (e.g., multiple arms) are reported in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: Because of the lack of relevant data, it was not possible to perform other meta-analyses, network meta-analysis, or individual patient data meta-analyses.
